MECHANICS LIEN PRELIMINARY NOTICE
Prepared for Acme Construction, Inc. · Jordan Alex Lee

PRELIMINARY NOTICE — PARTIES, PROPERTY, AND WORK FURNISHED
PRELIMINARY NOTICE
(Given pursuant to California Civil Code § 8200 et seq.)

From (Claimant): Acme Construction, Inc.

To (Owner or Reputed Owner): Jordan Alex Lee
Property: 123 Main St, Springfield

Direct Contractor (if other than Claimant): Beta Builders, LLC

Construction Lender (if any): _______________________________________________

Claimant first furnished labor, service, equipment, or materials to this work of improvement on: August 1, 2026

General description of the work provided or to be provided by Claimant: _______________________________________________

Estimate of the total price of the work provided and to be provided: $15,000

This notice is required by law as a statement of the sender's legal rights. It does not reflect on the financial condition of the contractor or of any person employed on this project.

WHO MAY CLAIM A MECHANICS LIEN
California law gives a mechanics lien right to a person who provides work authorized for a work of improvement, including — without limitation — a direct contractor, a subcontractor, a material supplier, an equipment lessor, a laborer, or a design professional (such as a licensed architect, landscape architect, engineer, or land surveyor who provides professional design services). A separate statute extends the same lien right to a person who provides authorized work for a site improvement (such as street, drainage, or utility work related to a subdivision) even where that work isn't part of a building's construction.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A person that provides work authorized for a work of improvement, including, but not limited to, the following persons, has a lien right under this chapter: (a) Direct contractor. (b) Subcontractor. (c) Material supplier. (d) Equipment lessor. (e) Laborer. (f) Design professional."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 8400 (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, persons who may claim a mechanics lien (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=8400.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of who California law recognizes as a potential lien claimant — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular project or contract. It states only that these categories of persons have a lien right; it doesn't state whether a specific person's work actually qualifies, whether that person is licensed as required for the work performed, or what amount, if any, that person could lawfully claim. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 8400); no additional independent source was found for this.

WHO MUST GIVE A PRELIMINARY NOTICE
Before recording a lien claim, giving a stop payment notice, or asserting a claim against a payment bond, California law generally requires a claimant to give a preliminary notice to the property's owner (or reputed owner), to the direct contractor (or reputed direct contractor) for the work — even if the claimant's own contract is with a subcontractor rather than the direct contractor — and to the construction lender, if any. Two categories of claimants are treated differently: a laborer is not required to give a preliminary notice at all, and a claimant who has a direct contractual relationship with the owner (which includes a direct contractor working directly for the owner) is required to give a preliminary notice only to the construction lender, if one exists — not to the owner or to a direct contractor.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "before recording a lien claim, giving a stop payment notice, or asserting a claim against a payment bond, a claimant shall give preliminary notice to the following persons: (1) The owner or reputed owner. (2) The direct contractor or reputed direct contractor to which the claimant provides work, either directly or through one or more subcontractors. (3) The construction lender or reputed construction lender, if any."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 8200(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, required recipients of a preliminary notice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=8200.)
  "Notwithstanding the foregoing subdivisions: (1) A laborer is not required to give preliminary notice. (2) A claimant with a direct contractual relationship with an owner or reputed owner is required to give preliminary notice only to the construction lender or reputed construction lender, if any."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 8200(e) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, exceptions for laborers and claimants in direct contractual privity with the owner (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=8200.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of who this state's law requires to give preliminary notice — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular project. The two quotes below are both subsections of the same statutory section (§ 8200) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this. It states the categories of required recipients and the two statutory exceptions; it doesn't state whether a specific claimant's contractual relationship with the owner is 'direct' for this purpose, whether a construction lender exists on a particular project, or what the consequence is for a specific claimant who omits a required recipient (that consequence is addressed in a separate section on lien-claim prerequisites, not restated here).

DEADLINE TO GIVE A PRELIMINARY NOTICE — AND THE PARTIAL-RECOVERY RULE FOR A LATE NOTICE
California law requires a preliminary notice to be given no later than 20 days after the claimant first furnishes work on the work of improvement. A claimant who misses that 20-day deadline is not permanently barred from giving a preliminary notice — the claimant may still give one at any time afterward. But a late notice limits recovery: the claimant may record a lien claim, give a stop payment notice, or assert a claim against a payment bond only for work performed within the 20 days immediately before the late notice was served, plus any work performed after that point. Work performed more than 20 days before a late preliminary notice is not recoverable through these remedies.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A preliminary notice shall be given not later than 20 days after the claimant has first furnished work on the work of improvement. If work has been provided by a claimant who did not give a preliminary notice, that claimant shall not be precluded from giving a preliminary notice at any time thereafter. The claimant shall, however, be entitled to record a lien, give a stop payment notice, and assert a claim against a payment bond only for work performed within 20 days prior to the service of the preliminary notice, and at any time thereafter."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 8204(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, 20-day preliminary notice deadline and partial-recovery rule for a late notice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=8204.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual, non-uniform preliminary-notice deadline and its partial-recovery consequence for a late notice — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular project's notice deadline. It doesn't state how 'first furnished work' is determined on a specific project, or address the separate rule for a design professional's preliminary notice (a design professional who notices within 20 days after the work of improvement commences is deemed compliant as to design services), which this document doesn't cover. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (§ 8204(a)); no additional independent source was found for this.

REQUIRED CONTENT OF A PRELIMINARY NOTICE, AND HOW IT MUST BE SERVED
A preliminary notice must include a general description of the work to be provided and an estimate of the total price of the work provided and to be provided, along with the general notice information California law requires (the owner's and direct contractor's names and addresses, the construction lender's name and address if any, a description of the site, and the person giving notice's name, address, and relationship to the parties). The notice must also include a specific boldface statutory warning addressed to the property owner, beginning 'NOTICE TO PROPERTY OWNER,' explaining that even full payment to the contractor doesn't protect against a lien for the claimant's unpaid work, and describing steps the owner may take to protect against that risk. Separately, California law specifies how notice under this part of the mechanics lien law must be given by mail: by registered mail, certified mail, express mail, or overnight delivery by an express service carrier.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "The preliminary notice shall comply with the requirements of Section 8102, and shall also include: (1) A general description of the work to be provided. (2) An estimate of the total price of the work provided and to be provided. (3) The following statement in boldface type: NOTICE TO PROPERTY OWNER EVEN THOUGH YOU HAVE PAID YOUR CONTRACTOR IN FULL, if the person or firm that has given you this notice is not paid in full for labor, service, equipment, or material provided or to be provided to your construction project, a lien may be placed on your property."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 8202(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, required content of a preliminary notice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=8202.)
  "Except as otherwise provided by this part, notice by mail under this part shall be given by registered or certified mail, express mail, or overnight delivery by an express service carrier."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 8110 (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, method of notice by mail (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=8110.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of this state's preliminary-notice content and mail-service requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular notice. The two citations below are from different statutory sections (§ 8202 and § 8110), not subsections of the same section. This document doesn't reproduce the complete boldface statutory warning text (see the drafting clause for that), doesn't address service methods other than mail (such as personal delivery, which this part also permits under a different section this document doesn't cover), and doesn't state when notice is deemed complete once sent (a separate section addresses that).

DEADLINE TO RECORD A MECHANICS LIEN CLAIM
The deadline to record a mechanics lien claim depends on the type of claimant. A direct contractor may not enforce a lien unless the claim of lien is recorded after the direct contract is completed and before the earlier of: 90 days after completion of the work of improvement, or 60 days after the owner records a notice of completion or notice of cessation. A claimant other than a direct contractor (a subcontractor, material supplier, equipment lessor, laborer, or design professional) may not enforce a lien unless the claim of lien is recorded after that claimant ceases to provide work and before the earlier of: 90 days after completion of the work of improvement, or 30 days after the owner records a notice of completion or notice of cessation. For this purpose, 'completion' of the work of improvement is a defined term with several possible triggers — including actual completion, the owner's occupation or use of the property together with cessation of labor, or a continuous 60-day cessation of labor — not simply the date construction work visibly ends.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A direct contractor may not enforce a lien unless the contractor records a claim of lien after the contractor completes the direct contract, and before the earlier of the following times: (a) Ninety days after completion of the work of improvement. (b) Sixty days after the owner records a notice of completion or cessation."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 8412 (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, direct contractor's deadline to record a lien claim (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=8412.)
  "A claimant other than a direct contractor may not enforce a lien unless the claimant records a claim of lien within the following times: (a) After the claimant ceases to provide work. (b) Before the earlier of the following times: (1) Ninety days after completion of the work of improvement. (2) Thirty days after the owner records a notice of completion or cessation."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 8414 (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, other claimants' deadline to record a lien claim (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=8414.)
  "For the purpose of this title, completion of a work of improvement occurs upon the occurrence of any of the following events: (1) Actual completion of the work of improvement. (2) Occupation or use by the owner accompanied by cessation of labor. (3) Cessation of labor for a continuous period of 60 days. (4) Recordation of a notice of cessation after cessation of labor for a continuous period of 30 days."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 8180(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, definition of 'completion' of a work of improvement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=8180.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of this state's lien-recording deadlines — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular project's deadline. The recording deadlines quoted are from two different sections (§ 8412 for a direct contractor, § 8414 for every other claimant) and the completion definition from a third (§ 8180); none are subsections of the same section. It states the general deadlines only; it doesn't state the deadline for a work of improvement performed under two or more separate direct contracts, which a different section addresses, and it doesn't state whether a notice of completion or notice of cessation was actually recorded on a particular project, which changes which of the alternative deadlines applies.

REQUIRED CONTENT, VERIFICATION, AND SERVICE OF A MECHANICS LIEN CLAIM
A claim of mechanics lien must be a written statement, signed and verified (made under oath) by the claimant, stating: the claimant's demand after deducting all just credits and offsets; the owner's or reputed owner's name, if known; a general statement of the kind of work furnished; the name of the person by whom the claimant was employed or to whom the claimant furnished work; a description of the site sufficient for identification; the claimant's address; a proof-of-service affidavit for service of the lien claim on the owner; and a specific boldface 'NOTICE OF MECHANICS LIEN' statutory warning. A copy of the recorded lien claim, including that warning, must also be served on the owner or reputed owner — generally by registered mail, certified mail, or first-class mail evidenced by a certificate of mailing, addressed to the owner's residence or place of business or to the address on file with the building permit authority (with an alternate method available if the owner cannot be served that way).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A claim of mechanics lien shall be a written statement, signed and verified by the claimant, containing all of the following: (1) A statement of the claimant's demand after deducting all just credits and offsets. (2) The name of the owner or reputed owner, if known. (3) A general statement of the kind of work furnished by the claimant. (4) The name of the person by whom the claimant was employed or to whom the claimant furnished work. (5) A description of the site sufficient for identification. (6) The claimant's address."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 8416(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, required content of a mechanics lien claim (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=8416.)
  "A copy of the claim of mechanics lien, which includes the Notice of Mechanics Lien required by paragraph (8) of subdivision (a), shall be served on the owner or reputed owner. Service shall be made as follows: (1) For an owner or reputed owner to be notified who resides in or outside this state, by registered mail, certified mail, or first-class mail, evidenced by a certificate of mailing, postage prepaid, addressed to the owner or reputed owner at the owner's or reputed owner's residence or place of business address or at the address shown by the building permit on file with the authority issuing a building permit for the work, or as otherwise provided in Section 8174."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 8416(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, service of the recorded lien claim on the owner (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=8416.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of this state's mechanics lien claim content and service requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular lien claim. The two citations below are both subsections of the same statutory section (§ 8416) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this. It doesn't reproduce the full boldface statutory warning text, doesn't state the amount a specific claimant may lawfully claim, and doesn't address the separate consequences of an inaccurate or overstated lien claim.

PRELIMINARY NOTICE — STATUTORY WARNING AND PROOF OF SERVICE
NOTICE TO PROPERTY OWNER

EVEN THOUGH YOU HAVE PAID YOUR CONTRACTOR IN FULL, if the person or firm that has given you this notice is not paid in full for labor, service, equipment, or material provided or to be provided to your construction project, a lien may be placed on your property. Foreclosure of the lien may lead to loss of all or part of your property. You may wish to protect yourself against this by (1) requiring your contractor to provide a signed release by the person or firm that has given you this notice before making payment to your contractor, or (2) any other method that is appropriate under the circumstances.

This notice is required by law to be served by the undersigned as a statement of your legal rights. This notice is not intended to reflect upon the financial condition of the contractor or the person employed by you on the construction project.

If you record a notice of cessation or completion of your construction project, you must within 10 days after recording, send a copy of the notice of completion to your contractor and the person or firm that has given you this notice. The notice must be sent by registered or certified mail. Failure to send the notice will extend the deadline to record a claim of lien. You are not required to send the notice if you are a residential homeowner of a dwelling containing four or fewer units.

Claimant: Acme Construction, Inc.
Signature: _______________________ Date: _______________

PROOF OF SERVICE
This notice was served on Jordan Alex Lee on _______________, by (check one):
☐ Registered mail   ☐ Certified mail   ☐ Express mail   ☐ Overnight delivery by an express service carrier
addressed to: _______________________________________________

Served by: _______________________________________________

NOTICE TO PROPERTY OWNER

EVEN THOUGH YOU HAVE PAID YOUR CONTRACTOR IN FULL, if the person or firm that has given you this notice is not paid in full for labor, service, equipment, or material provided or to be provided to your construction project, a lien may be placed on your property. Foreclosure of the lien may lead to loss of all or part of your property. You may wish to protect yourself against this by (1) requiring your contractor to provide a signed release by the person or firm that has given you this notice before making payment to your contractor, or (2) any other method that is appropriate under the circumstances.

This notice is required by law to be served by the undersigned as a statement of your legal rights. This notice is not intended to reflect upon the financial condition of the contractor or the person employed by you on the construction project.

If you record a notice of cessation or completion of your construction project, you must within 10 days after recording, send a copy of the notice of completion to your contractor and the person or firm that has given you this notice. The notice must be sent by registered or certified mail. Failure to send the notice will extend the deadline to record a claim of lien. You are not required to send the notice if you are a residential homeowner of a dwelling containing four or fewer units.

Claimant: Acme Construction, Inc.
Signature: _______________________ Date: _______________

PROOF OF SERVICE
